steps.title: Text A · Fourteen days I had not agreed to
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Until two years ago I had never slept anywhere without a lock on the door. I was not an adventurous person and I had never pretended to be one. My holidays were cities, museums and a return flight booked before I left. Then my sister paid for a fourteen-day trek through a remote valley in the north, told me afterwards, and refused to discuss it. Her argument was that I needed to step out of my comfort zone. Mine was that I had a job, a cat and no boots.

By the end of the first afternoon I had already stopped speaking. We had been walking for six hours, my bag weighed more than I had estimated, and the physical side of it was worse than anything I had prepared for. Nobody had warned me that the difficulty of a trek is not the distance but the small decisions: whether to stop now or in twenty minutes, whether the pain in your heel is a blister or the boot. My sister, who had done this sort of thing before, made a poor companion that first day. She kept pointing out that the views were stunning, which they were, and which did not help.

The trip turned on day four. We had lost the path an hour earlier and had been arguing about the map when an old man appeared from nowhere with two dogs. Neither of us spoke his language and he had no interest in ours. He looked at the map, laughed at it, and walked us to the col. There he pointed at our destination, a white village on the far side of the valley, and went home. The whole encounter lasted less than an hour and it is the only part of the fortnight I would call remarkable. Neither of us had done anything to deserve it.

steps.title: Text B · What it was not
steps.html:
Written for this course.

What surprised me afterwards was how little of it was about courage. I finished the walk because turning back had become more trouble than going on, and that is not the same thing. There was no moment on any of the fourteen days when I chose the difficult option over the easy one; there was simply never an easy one available. People who describe a trek as a feat, or who come home calling themselves explorers, have usually skipped that part of the story. Nobody had sent us on a mission. We were two women with a map neither of us could read.

Something did change, though, and it changed later than I expected. By the second week I had taken over the route, the food and the timing, not out of determination but because my sister had stopped doing it and somebody had to. I was carrying a responsibility I had spent forty years arranging my life to avoid, and it turned out to weigh about as much as the bag. On the last evening I wandered round a town I had never heard of, alone, in the dark, for two hours, and enjoyed every minute of it.

I am not a different person. I still book the return flight first, and I have not thrown away the lock on the door. But I am determined to go back, and this time I have booked it myself, which my sister says proves her point and which I am not going to admit. If she had asked me first, I would have said no, and I would have been wrong; I am prepared to accept that much and no more.

steps.title: Past simple, past continuous, used to / would
steps.html:
The three forms a past narrative runs on — and the first sight of a fourth.

The past simple carries the events, in the order they happened: I said yes. We wandered off the path. She hit the crocodile. This is the backbone of every story.

The past continuous sets the scene around those events, or describes something already in progress when one of them happened: Liz was reading the map when we got lost. The longer action takes -ing; the interrupting one takes the past simple.

Used to and would describe repeated past habits that are over. We used to camp every summer. We would drive through the night. Only used to works for past states: I used to be afraid of heights — not I would be afraid.

And then there is the fourth: past perfect. When you need to reach back to something that happened before the point your story has reached, you use had + past participle: The first day was physical in a way I had not expected. Lesson 10 takes this apart properly.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the two accounts.

A friend asked me to be her companion.
Past simple — one event.

I said yes for the worst possible reason.
Past simple — the next event.

The destination moved further away each time I looked at the map.
Two past simples, one after the other.

By the evening I had stopped talking altogether.
Past perfect — earlier than the evening.

I had slept badly and I had eaten almost nothing.
Past perfect — both before the second day began.

Somewhere on the climb I found a kind of determination.
Past simple — the turning point.

Past simple with a definite date.

Her father's friends had warned her. She ignored them.
The warning came first, so past perfect, then past simple.

She was travelling by canoe when the crocodile appeared.
Past continuous for the longer action, past simple for the interruption.

The skirt she had refused to give up saved her legs.
The refusal came first.

She used to write to her brother every week.
A repeated past habit, now over.

They would set off before it got light.
Would for a habit — but never for a state.

1. The raw facts: (1) she booked the trek, (2) she told me, (3) I agreed. In that order.

  4. Anything happening around the moment goes into the past continuous: We were sitting in her kitchen when she told me.
  5. Put it together: We were sitting in her kitchen when she told me. She had already booked it. I agreed. Three forms, three jobs.

  • Use the past continuous at least once for something in progress.
  • Use the past perfect at least once for something that happened earlier.
  • Close with what the trip actually cost you, or gave you.

Useful language

  • I am not a particularly adventurous person, but …
  • I said yes because …
  • We were …-ing when …
  • By the second day I had …
  • It took no courage at all to … ; what it took was …
  • I would not do it again, but I am glad I did.
steps.modelHtml:
The night bus to Osh

I am not a particularly adventurous traveller. I like knowing where I will sleep. So I still do not entirely understand why I agreed to take a night bus over the mountains to Osh with a colleague I had met four days earlier.

We left at nine. By midnight the heating had failed, and everyone on the bus was wearing everything they had brought. I was trying to sleep against the window when the driver stopped, opened the door and walked off into the dark without explaining anything at all.

He came back twenty minutes later with bread. He had been to a house he knew. Nobody else on the bus seemed remotely surprised.

It took no courage to get on that bus, because I had no idea what I was agreeing to. What it took was the twelve hours afterwards.
